overview: Bagan, also called Pagan, was the center of a powerful kingdom in the Ayeyarwady valley of present-day Myanmar. This atlas record isolates 1200 to 1279, part of its late flourishing, rather than the kingdom’s whole lifetime. The imported polygon actually excludes Bagan and Kyaukse while including Mrauk U and Chittagong. It is geographically misleading and cannot establish the kingdom’s borders. Earlier Pagan and the later Pagan map record remain separate here; the change of label in 1279 was not the disappearance of the city.

periods.title: The atlas’s late Bagan interval
periods.summary: Temple patronage and a working settlement landscape continued during this selected map phase.

periods.title: Political change beyond the map seam
periods.summary: The kingdom fragmented in the late thirteenth century; religious life continued.

sections.title: A capital built by many kinds of work

items.text: Bagan’s kings connected religious patronage with the organization of land, labor and building. Agricultural production helped support monasteries and monuments, while royal sponsorship also shaped trade. Historian Rila Mukherjee emphasizes these connections: a glittering temple depended on fields and workers as well as a generous donor.

The early thirteenth-century Htilominlo Temple rises in two storeys around a massive solid core. Its builders combined brickwork with sandstone blocks. A big temple had to solve a very practical puzzle: how to carry the weight of the upper shrine without squashing the spaces beneath it.

The walls enclosed Bagan’s royal and religious center, not its entire population. Archaeologists study a surrounding mixture of homes, farmland and religious buildings. Timber and other perishable domestic materials leave fainter traces than brick temples, which helps explain why spectacular monuments long received more attention than ordinary households.

At Shwe Creek, excavators found plastered and tamped-earth floors, postholes and objects lying on former living surfaces. Radiocarbon results place early and middle activity within 1045 to 1216 and later activity within 1254 to 1295. These ranges overlap this card’s century but do not date every floor to one precise year.

Shwe Creek also produced pottery-making tools, including ceramic anvils and a spacer, alongside many broken pots. The excavators interpret the place as a possible combination of residence and pottery production. For some occupants, getting to work may have involved a very short commute.

sections.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives

items.text: Bagan-period inscriptions name parents, spouses, children, stepmothers and in-laws. They distinguish a mother’s older sister from her younger sister. A short stone record can contain quite a family tree.

The records distinguish rice cooks from curry cooks, as well as household cooks, fish suppliers and honey suppliers. Preparing a communal meal could involve several specialized jobs. Communal cooking required teamwork.

Occupational names also include midwives, laundresses and water carriers. Singers, dancers, drummers and cymbal players appear among the musical professions. These inscriptions preserve childbirth care and entertainment alongside the better-known labor of building temples.

This work was not always freely chosen. Inscriptions describe people inherited, bought or transferred to settle debts. Than Tun records a palm-leaf preparer whose bankruptcy in 1227 brought his family into enslavement under a minister. Religious monuments also belonged to this unequal society.

A later record, from 1291, required monks to care for people dedicated to a monastery when they became sick or old. It records an obligation, not proof that everyone received good treatment. The date also falls beyond this map interval.

Food archaeology reaches further back. At Otein Taung, pigs’ teeth and ruminant bones came from an ash layer dated to 880 to 1030. The excavators suggested meals were cooked on the hot ashes. This is a glimpse of earlier activity near Bagan, not a menu securely dated to the thirteenth century.

Bagan’s waterworks linked seasonal channels, ponds and reservoirs in a dry landscape. The excavated moat stood above the nearby river’s level, so rainwater was important to filling it. Managing the arrival and storage of water mattered as much as standing beside a great river.

Possible ancient toilets are among the less glamorous discoveries. At Old Bagan, excavators found earthenware tubes stacked vertically, sometimes eight deep, interpreted as latrine linings. Similar fragments occurred at Otein Taung. The report does not securely date these installations to this card’s century; a clay-lined pit is also not evidence for a citywide sewer network.

More than fifty spouts from ritual water-pouring pots were collected on Otein Taung’s surface. Smaller numbers were excavated below. Such vessels connected pottery manufacture to Buddhist offerings. A broken spout can tell archaeologists what sort of pot it belonged to, even when most of the pot has vanished.

Writing and religious learning were not confined entirely to men. Rachelle Saruya’s review identifies Bagan-period inscriptions describing some literate enslaved women and nuns learned in Buddhist ritual. Later chronicles praise women’s study of Pali grammar, but those stories cannot establish how many medieval girls attended school.

At Payathonzu, probably a thirteenth-century temple, paintings display an elaborate late Bagan style. The museum catalogue describes compositions with the Buddha inside a structure resembling the temple at Bodh Gaya. Artists used recognizable sacred settings to connect a local place of worship with a much wider Buddhist world.

sections.title: A traveler’s gift and words carved in stone

items.text: A sandstone inscription found at Myinpagan records a donor from Magodayarpattanam on India’s Malabar coast. He provided a hall, a door and a lamp to burn continually in a Vishnu temple at Bagan. Its Sanskrit verse and Tamil prose reveal a specific South Indian religious connection within this predominantly Buddhist city.

The same inscription begins “Svasti śrî,” translated by its editor as “Hail! Prosperity!” These are the published Roman-letter transliteration of Sanskrit words carved in Grantha script, not a facsimile of the letters. The Tamil letterforms date the stone approximately to the thirteenth century. This witness represents one donor’s dedication, not everyone’s everyday language.

ending.text: The 1279 map seam is not a fall date. Bagan’s kingdom fragmented in the late thirteenth century and other centers gained power. Mongol pressure belonged to this upheaval, but a story of total destruction of the city is not supported by the evidence. Bagan continued as a place of worship, with later rebuilding and living Buddhist communities.
